newsitem.title: USA: Clinton signals possible deal on Social Security.
newsitem.headline: Clinton signals possible deal on Social Security.

text.p: President Bill Clinton, seeking ways to help balance the budget, raised the prospect Saturday of a compromise with congressional Republicans on curbing cost-of-living increases for Social Security recipients.
Cinton, in an interview to be broadcast Sunday on CBS's "Face the Nation," said he could consider such curbs to cut spending, possibly paving the way for a balanced budget deal.

The president, preparing to kick off a national service summit in Philadelphia Sunday, also said he would send a bill to Congress Monday exempting student volunteers from paying interest on their student loans during the time they serve.

Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, who urged Clinton Friday to make "a really bold move" on the budget, has left open the possibility of a compromise on the politically explosive Consumer Price Index issue -- if the president would consider it.

Lott has been pressing for a downward adjustment in the Consumer Price Index, used to calculate the cost of living increases for government benefits such as Social Security, tax-rate brackets and wages.
Lowering the index would mean a smaller increase in Social Security and other benefits, potentially saving the government tens of billions of dollars.
Clinton, in the interview taped Saturday, said he could weigh such a spending curb "if it's justified."

He noted that "most people believe that the cost-of-living formula the government now uses overstates the real cost of living to the people who benefit from the programs. There is an overwhelming consensus about that."

"So, let me reiterate what I have said repeatedly: I think there ought to be a cost-of-living adjustment. But it ought to be accurate," Clinton said, noting there was "significant disagreement" over the exact level the CPI should be.

The White House and congressional Republicans are locked in negotiations over how to balance the budget by 2002, with the key issues including the size of a tax cut and the extent of cuts to the Medicare health care program for the elderly.

Sen. John Breaux, a Democrat from Louisiana, told CNN's "Inside Politics Weekend" the two sides were "very, very close" to reaching agreement on a balanced budget deal and an accord could be announced by next weekend.

He said the deal would likely involve a compromise on the size of a tax cut, a "reasonable" CPI adjustment and splitting the difference between the economic assumptions of the Office of Management and Budget and the Congressional Budget Office.
"I think we're very close," Breaux said.

But a fiscal conservative, Sen. Phil Gramm, a Texas Republican who was instrumental in defeating Clinton's health care reform during his first term, vowed to "savage" any deal to cut Social Security on the floor of the Senate.

"If we see an agreement ... to politicize the Consumer Price Index, to cut Social Security and raise taxes under the table, I am going to savage it on the floor of the United States Senate and we're going to have one hell of a fight about it," Gramm told CNN on the same program.
An advisory commission headed by Stanford University economist Michael Boskin late last year said the CPI overstated inflation by about 1.1 percentage points a year.

Republicans last week made a proposal that moved in the direction of the White House on the size of proposed tax cuts and on Medicare spending reductions, but were still far from Clinton's proposal. Lott said they were awaiting a reply.
Clinton said his bill to exempt volunteers from student loan interest made good sense.
"If they are willing to give something to their country, it seems to me just the least we can do is relieve them of a burden of the interest accumulating during that period," he told CBS.
